introduction-why-grep-fails-at-scale.core: grep scans every byte on every query, so cost grows with the size of the codebase. At thousands of repositories you need a pre-built index that answers queries without scanning.

first_principles.problem: Searching 5,000 repos with grep takes minutes per query, and nobody can find where a deprecated API is still used.
truths: Scanning cost is proportional to data size.
Indexes trade build time for fast lookups.
derivation: Build an **index once** (and update it incrementally).
Answer queries by **index lookup**, then verify candidates.

analogy.title: A library with 5,000 rooms
analogy.story: Reading every book per question is impossible; a card catalogue points straight to the right shelves.
analogy.breaks: Indexes go stale and must be kept in sync with the repositories.

check.q: Why does grep get slower as the codebase grows?
check.a: It scans every byte for each query, so time grows linearly with code size.

indexing-strategies-trigrams-n-grams.core: Code isn't made of words, so code search indexes every 3-character substring (trigram) along with where it occurs. A query is split into trigrams, their posting lists are intersected to find candidate files, and only those files are verified.

first_principles.problem: Word-based indexes fail on code like `getUserById(` or `->conn`, where tokens aren't natural-language words.
truths: Any substring of 3+ characters contains trigrams.

analogy.title: Finding a word using letter-triplet cards
analogy.story: Pull the cards for 'log', 'ogi' and 'gin'. Only books on all three cards can contain 'login'.
analogy.breaks: Queries shorter than three characters can't use the index efficiently.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only 1.2k files are scanned instead of millions.

check.q: Why trigrams rather than words for code?
check.a: Code identifiers and symbols don't split into natural words, but every substring of 3+ characters contains trigrams.

regex-and-structural-search.core: Regex queries are accelerated by pulling out their literal fragments as trigram filters before running the full regex on candidates. Structural search (Comby, Semgrep) matches code shapes with holes, independent of formatting.

first_principles.problem: Developers search for patterns ('functions returning err without wrapping'), not exact strings.
truths: Code structure is independent of whitespace.
Pattern templates can capture parts of code.
derivation: Extract **required literals** from the regex and filter by trigrams.

analogy.title: A pre-filter then a microscope
analogy.story: A coarse sieve removes most sand; the microscope checks what remains.
analogy.breaks: Regexes with no literals (`.*`) can't be accelerated and fall back to scanning.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: It matches across line breaks and formatting styles.

code.text:
Comby: return :[_], err
excluding: return :[_], fmt.Errorf(:[_])

example.outcome: pattern searches across all code are precise and fast.

check.q: How does a code search engine speed up a regex query?
check.a: It extracts required literal substrings, uses the trigram index to find candidates, then runs the regex only on them.

how-a-real-code-search-system-is-assembl.core: A production code search system has repo syncers, indexers building trigram shards, sharded index servers, a query planner that fans out and merges ranked results, and a UI or API, often with symbol and cross-reference data added.

first_principles.problem: The components only add up to a useful tool once they're composed into a fast, fresh, scalable pipeline.
truths: Indexes must be sharded to scale.
derivation: **Sync** repos on push or a schedule.
**Fan out** queries to shards and **merge and rank**.
Add **symbols and code intel** (SCIP) for go-to-definition across repos.

analogy.title: A newspaper archive service
analogy.story: Couriers bring new editions, archivists index them into volumes, and a librarian queries all volumes and presents the best articles first.
analogy.breaks: Freshness costs compute. There's always some indexing lag.

example.outcome: the whole organisation's code is searchable instantly.

check.q: Why are code search indexes sharded?
check.a: To spread data and query load across machines so search scales with the size of the codebase.
